learn.hook: Whoosh! Swoosh! Can you hear a poem? Some poems are made to be heard as much as read!
points: 'The Kites' is a poem about the joy and colour of kites flying in the sky.
Onomatopoeia: words that sound like what they describe (whoosh, swoosh, flutter, snap).
Alliteration: the same first sound repeated in words close together ('bright, breezy day').
Personification: kites 'go dancing', as if they were people. A metaphor: 'The sky is a garden.'
Rhyme and rhythm make a poem feel like the swaying, rising and dipping of a kite.

example.q: Read this original poem: Up on the roof on a bright, breezy day, / Red kites and green kites go dancing away; / The string in my hand hums whoosh, whoosh, whoosh, / As up goes my kite with a swoop and a swoosh. / "Kai po che!" shouts my cousin with glee — / The sky is a garden as far as I see. Find one example each of onomatopoeia, alliteration and metaphor.
steps: 'The sky is a garden' calls the sky a garden without 'like' → metaphor.
example.answer: Onomatopoeia: whoosh/swoosh; alliteration: bright, breezy; metaphor: the sky is a garden.

learn.reallife: On kite-flying days, rooftops fill with shouts, whistles and the whirr of the spool — a real-life sound poem!

quiz.q: In the kite poem, where is the speaker?
quiz.explain: Line 1 says 'Up on the roof'.
quiz.mistake: Does not use the first line as the setting

quiz.q: "Red kites and green kites go dancing away". Kites cannot really dance, so this is:
quiz.explain: Giving kites a human action (dancing) is personification.

quiz.q: Which words in the poem are examples of onomatopoeia?
quiz.explain: 'Whoosh' and 'swoosh' imitate the sound of rushing air.

quiz.q: 'bright, breezy day' is an example of:
quiz.explain: Two nearby words begin with the same 'b' sound.

quiz.q: In the poem, "The sky is a garden as far as I see." Why is the sky called a garden?
options: It has real plants growing in it
It is full of many colourful kites, like flowers
quiz.explain: Colourful kites dotting the sky look like flowers in a garden.

quiz.q: In the poem, the cousin shouts 'Kai po che!' with glee. 'Glee' means:
quiz.explain: Glee is great delight or joy.

quiz.q: Which pair rhymes in the poem?
quiz.explain: 'Glee' and 'see' end in the same '-ee' sound.
quiz.mistake: Picks words that do not share an ending sound

quiz.q: What feeling does the kite poem mainly show?
quiz.explain: Dancing kites, sound words and shouts of glee show joy.
quiz.mistake: Does not read the mood of the words

teach.ask: Gappu hears 'whoosh, swoosh' and asks: 'Why does this poem sound like the wind?'
teach.praise: Tweet! Sound words like whoosh are onomatopoeia — the poem makes the sound of the wind!
teach.nudge: What do we call words that sound like what they mean?

learn.hook: In January, the skies over many Indian cities fill with thousands of kites. Which festival is it?
points: Makar Sankranti, in January, marks the sun's movement into Makara (Capricorn). It is a harvest-time festival celebrated across India by different names.
In Gujarat it is called Uttarayan, and people fly kites from rooftops all day. Ahmedabad hosts a famous International Kite Festival.
In Tamil Nadu the same season brings Pongal; in Punjab, Lohri is celebrated the night before Makar Sankranti; in Assam, it is Magh (Bhogali) Bihu.
Kites are also flown on Independence Day (15 August) in Delhi and other places.
Kite safety: never use glass-coated or nylon string (manja) — it hurts birds and people; stay away from electric wires; fly only from safe places with an adult nearby.

example.q: Think it through: Rehan wants to fly kites on Uttarayan with glass-coated manja from the edge of the roof near an electric wire. What three things should he change?
steps: Glass-coated manja can cut birds and people → use plain cotton thread.
The edge of the roof is dangerous → stay in a safe, railed area with an adult.
Electric wires are dangerous → fly far away from them.
example.answer: Use plain cotton thread, stay in a safe place with an adult, and keep away from electric wires.

learn.reallife: Bird hospitals and volunteers in Gujarat work extra hard during Uttarayan to help birds hurt by sharp manja — safe string saves lives.

games.title: Kite safety
items: Sharp string cuts the wings of birds.
It is safe to fly kites near electric wires.
Kites and strings can get tangled in live wires — very dangerous.
Children should fly kites from rooftops with an adult nearby.
An adult helps keep rooftop flying safe.
Running on a busy road to catch a cut kite is fine.
Never run onto roads chasing kites.
Cotton thread is safer than glass-coated string.
Plain cotton thread is much safer.

quiz.q: In which state is Makar Sankranti called Uttarayan?
quiz.explain: In Gujarat, the festival is called Uttarayan and is famous for kite flying.

quiz.q: In which month is Makar Sankranti celebrated?
quiz.explain: Makar Sankranti falls in January.

quiz.q: Which city hosts a famous International Kite Festival?
quiz.explain: Ahmedabad in Gujarat hosts the International Kite Festival around Uttarayan.
quiz.mistake: Does not link kites with Gujarat

quiz.q: Lohri is celebrated mainly in:
quiz.explain: Lohri is a winter festival of Punjab, celebrated the night before Makar Sankranti.

quiz.q: Why should we avoid glass-coated manja?
options: It makes kites fly too low
It can cut and hurt birds and people
quiz.explain: Sharp string injures birds and people.
quiz.mistake: Does not know the danger of sharp string

quiz.q: Your kite gets stuck on an electric wire. What should you do?
options: Throw a metal rod at it
Leave it and tell an adult
quiz.explain: Electric wires can give dangerous shocks; leave it and inform an adult.
quiz.mistake: Takes a dangerous risk to save a kite

quiz.q: On which day are kites flown in Delhi as part of the celebrations?
quiz.explain: Kite flying is a popular Independence Day tradition in Delhi.

quiz.q: Makar Sankranti marks the sun's movement into:
quiz.explain: 'Makar' refers to Makara, the zodiac sign Capricorn.
quiz.mistake: Does not know the meaning of the festival's name

teach.ask: Gappu is worried: 'Kite festival is coming! It looks fun, but I'm a bird — will I be safe?'
teach.praise: Tweet! Fly kites with safe cotton thread, away from wires, with an adult. Then birds and kids are all happy!
teach.nudge: What kind of string should people use so that birds like me don't get hurt?

learn.hook: Look up! The kites ARE FLYING, my cousin IS SHOUTING and I AM HOLDING the string — all right now!
points: The present continuous tense describes an action happening now: am/is/are + verb + -ing.
I am flying; he/she/it is flying; we/you/they are flying.
Spelling: most verbs add -ing (fly → flying); drop silent -e (make → making); double the last letter after a short vowel (run → running); -ie becomes -y (tie → tying).
Negative: am/is/are + not + -ing ('She is not flying a kite'). Question: Am/Is/Are + subject + -ing? ('Are you flying a kite?')
Verbs of thinking and feeling such as know, like, want, believe are usually NOT used in the continuous: say 'I know', not 'I am knowing'.

example.q: Think it through: Change to the present continuous: 'My cousin cuts the kite and shouts.'
example.answer: My cousin is cutting the kite and shouting.

learn.reallife: Live cricket commentary is full of it: 'He is running in, he is bowling... and the batter is hitting it for six!'

items.text: Look! The kites ___ in the sky.
They ___ in the park right now.

quiz.q: Choose the present continuous: 'Ravi ___ a kite now.'
quiz.explain: 'Now' shows an action in progress; Ravi is singular → is flying.
quiz.mistake: Uses the simple present or past for an action happening now

quiz.q: What is the correct -ing form of 'run'?
quiz.explain: Short verbs ending in one vowel + one consonant double the consonant: running.

quiz.q: What is the -ing form of 'make'?
quiz.explain: Drop the silent -e before adding -ing.

quiz.q: Which sentence uses the verb 'know' correctly?
quiz.explain: 'Know' is a thinking verb and is not usually used in the continuous.
quiz.mistake: Uses a thinking verb in the continuous tense

quiz.q: Make it negative: 'She is flying a kite.'
options: She not is flying a kite.
She does not flying a kite.
She is not fly a kite.
She is not flying a kite.
quiz.explain: Put 'not' after 'is' and keep the -ing verb.

quiz.q: Make it a question: 'They are watching the kites.'
quiz.explain: Put 'Are' before the subject: Are they watching...?

quiz.q: Fill in: 'We ___ for the bus at the moment.'
quiz.explain: 'We' takes 'are'; 'at the moment' shows an action now.
quiz.mistake: Uses the wrong helping verb for the subject

quiz.q: Which time phrase usually goes with the present continuous?
quiz.explain: 'Right now' shows an action in progress.
quiz.mistake: Confuses habits or past time with the present continuous

teach.ask: Gappu chirps: 'I am flying, I am singing, I am learning! What tense is this?'
teach.praise: Tweet! Am, is, are plus -ing tells what's happening right now. I am loving... oops, I love it!
teach.nudge: What helping words and what ending do we need for the present continuous?
